extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners designing or evaluating peer-grading systems (instructors, MOOC/platform designers, learning scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence about how to assign reviewers and how many reviewers to use in peer-grading systems, focusing on effects on accuracy, fairness, workload, and learning. Synthesizes empirical findings and design patterns across classroom and MOOC contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random Reviewer Assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review tasks are assigned randomly, without considering specific reviewer attributes or qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple and scalable; commonly used (~75% of systems). Problems include inconsistent grading, fairness concerns (low-quality reviewers unevenly assigned), and missing reviews. Mitigations include adding calibration papers, dynamic allocation to submissions with fewest reviews, priority mechanisms (boost for active reviewers), and mixing random assignment with other strategies (e.g., draw from least-reviewed). Examples: Chakraborty et al.’s calibration mix; CrowdGrader selection from least-reviewed submissions; Staubitz et al. priority boosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency-Based Reviewer Assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign reviewers based on indicators of expertise or reliability (academic performance, domain knowledge, past grading behavior, calibration accuracy, topic similarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can systematically mitigate skewed grading and fairness problems. Implementations include clustering students by cognitive indicators, enforcing calibration thresholds (e.g., ≥60% agreement) to unlock review privileges, and creating skill-based pools (high/medium/low). Best practice: assign multiple reviewers from different competency levels to each submission to ensure diverse perspectives and fairness (one high, one medium, one random). Risks: may promote meritocracy, depends on valid competency measures, and requires available performance data (more feasible in classrooms). Examples: Bhavya et al., Haddidi et al., Boudria et al., Badea et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Network-Based Reviewer Assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use social interaction data (forum replies/votes/follows, prior interactions, class membership) to guide reviewer assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptually can improve fairness and objectivity by leveraging interaction traces; observed mainly in MOOCs where interaction data are abundant. Potential uses: avoid assigning classmates or use social proximity metrics. Empirical evidence is limited and further statistical evaluation is needed. Examples: Chiou et al. (forum-based metrics), Jingjing et al. (avoid classmates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidding-Based Reviewer Assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow students to select which assignments they wish to review (bidding/choice-based assignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May speed grading and increase early engagement since peers self-assign; systems often impose minimum review counts and incentives (e.g., reward points that decay after a threshold) to prevent redundant grading or cherry-picking. Risks: potential for skewed attention to 'attractive' submissions; requires mechanisms (thresholds, anonymity) to maintain coverage and fairness. Example: Alipour et al. implementation with anonymous submissions and decreasing reward points after three reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity (single-blind, double-blind, onymous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewer and/or author identities are concealed affects feedback style and social dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity tends to encourage more critical feedback and reduce social pressure, but can reduce accountability, trust, and interpersonal engagement. Designers should weigh trade-offs between candid criticism and accountability/engagement depending on pedagogical goals. (Panadero et al. empirical review findings cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of Reviewers per Submission
rubrics_metrics.description: How many peer reviews each submission receives (commonly reported values: 3 is most common; typical recommended range 3–5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing reviewer count generally improves grading accuracy and reliability, but with diminishing returns: sharp gains up to ~4–5, moderate gains 5–8, and marginal gains beyond. Many studies find 3–5 reviews balance accuracy, student workload, learning outcomes, and engagement; >5 risks disengagement or rushed reviews. Minimum validity often requires ≥2–3 reviewers. Examples: Price et al. (three reviewers achieve R2 > 0.8), Capuano et al. and Nakayama et al. reported diminishing returns beyond 5–6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of calibration papers or calibration tasks to measure/adjust reviewer accuracy before or during peer grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibration can substantially reduce grading error (e.g., Yuan et al. reported up to 39.13 MSE-point reduction). Calibration can be used to unlock review privileges, compute weights, or train reviewers. Calibration thresholds (e.g., ≥60% agreement with instructor) are used in some systems. Use calibration especially when relying on random assignment to mitigate harsh/lenient graders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting by Reliability / Reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight reviewers’ contributions based on reliability metrics (calibration scores, reputation, past grading quality, engagement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighting improves aggregated accuracy and can incentivize high-quality feedback (meritocratic effects). Implementations include reliability-weighted assignment, personalized weights from engagement/performance, and Individual Weighting Factor methods. Be aware of fairness implications of rewarding already advantaged graders. Examples: García-Martínez et al., Chan et al., James et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic Allocation / Adaptive Assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate or reallocate reviews dynamically in response to current review coverage or reviewer behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigates missing or uneven reviews by drawing submissions with fewest current reviews when a reviewer begins a new review. Helps balance workload and ensures coverage (e.g., Andriamiseza et al., CrowdGrader). Can be combined with competency-based matching or priority mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of Reviewer Competency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure each submission is reviewed by a mix of reviewers from different competency or reputation levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning reviewers from high, medium, and low skill pools produces more balanced, complementary feedback and improves fairness. Methods include deliberate sampling from multiple skill pools or enforcing at-least-one-from-each-level rules. Examples: Jiménez-Romero et al., Badea et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority / Incentive Mechanisms for Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Incentives that adjust future assignment probability or rewards based on reviewer participation/quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms such as giving priority to students who submitted reviews increase likelihood their own work is reviewed and incentivize active participation. Incentives can be coupled with reputation and reward-point decay to shape engagement (Staubitz et al., Alipour et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Pools and Threshold-based Access
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizing reviewers into pools (e.g., independent vs supervised; high/medium/low) and using thresholds (e.g., calibration pass) to determine pool membership or access to review tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pool-based designs allow targeted assignment strategies (e.g., independent pool reviews similar-competence peers; supervised pool for lower-accuracy reviewers) and can increase grading reliability when pool definitions are valid. Examples: Wright et al., Boudria et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid Models (peer + TA/expert grading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating some TA or instructor grading with peer reviews to adjust or anchor peer-assigned grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid approaches (e.g., mixing TA-graded scores or seeding expert-graded calibration items) can produce reliable results with fewer peer reviews and help correct systemic bias. Useful when full expert grading is infeasible but occasional expert input is available (e.g., Fang et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation Methods and Statistical Models
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of aggregation/estimation method (arithmetic mean, ordinal aggregation, Bayesian inference, IRT, rank aggregation) to combine peer judgments into final scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some aggregation methods can achieve high accuracy with fewer reviewers (e.g., Bayesian inference, ordinal models). Designers should select aggregation approaches matched to rating scales and noise characteristics. Examples: Caragiannis et al., Zarkoob et al., Raman & Joachims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student Workload and Engagement Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: How many reviews each student must perform, and the resulting impact on engagement, perceived workload, and review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning more than five reviews per student risks disengagement or superficial reviews; three reviews is often seen as reasonable and beneficial. Balance the educational benefit of reviewing with time cost to students. Consider caps (e.g., ≤5) and designs that sustain engagement across assignments (Lee et al., Mi & Yeung).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy vs Workload Trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Design trade-off between improved grading accuracy (more reviewers) and increased reviewer workload (more time for students).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence suggests major accuracy gains up to ~4–5 reviewers and diminishing returns thereafter. Common recommendation: 3–5 reviews per submission to balance reliability, workload, and learning outcomes. Use weighting/calibration to reduce required reviewer counts while maintaining accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and Context Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical feasibility of assignment strategy given context (MOOC vs classroom), available data, and system scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random assignment is highly scalable and common in MOOCs; competency-based and pool strategies are more feasible in traditional classrooms where richer learner data are available. Consider computational and data-collection costs when choosing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality / Evaluation Metrics for Peer-Grading Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures used to evaluate peer-grading outcomes: accuracy (RMSE, MAE), correlation/R^2 with expert grades, reliability, fairness, timeliness, and reviewer workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective metrics (RMSE, MAE, R^2) to compare schemes and report trade-offs (e.g., Caragiannis, Kulkarni, Price). Also include qualitative measures like perceived educational value, engagement, and fairness from student feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and Fairness Mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of how assignment strategies can introduce or exacerbate bias (e.g., uneven distribution of low-quality reviewers) and approaches to mitigate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include competency matching, enforced reviewer diversity, calibration and weighting, dynamic reallocation, and transparent policies. Monitor for cases where submissions receive no evaluations and design fallback mechanisms (e.g., reassign missing reviews). Examples: Toll et al., Albano et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Rigorous Empirical Validation and Identified Research Gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that many promising strategies (especially social-network and bidding-based assignments, and hybrid strategies) lack large-scale, controlled empirical comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers and researchers should conduct large-scale studies isolating assignment effects, empirically evaluate hybrid models, and test strategies across contexts (MOOC vs classroom). Consider including non-English and gray literature and documenting context-specific variables (assignment type, submission length) when reporting results.
